title: Clear a platform-game level with a real gamepad: hold the stick for full speed, time the jumps, hold A for height
instruction: Use the game controller to get the character to the flag.
context: Playing a console game with a gamepad is everyday leisure: 43% of U.S. adults often or sometimes play video games and 39% own a games console (Pew Research Center, 2018); 205.1 million Americans aged 5-90 play regularly (ESA, 2025). A platform level is a two-handed timing knack: one thumb holds the stick past 90% of its 21-degree throw for full speed (nothing moves inside 20%) while the other presses A at the right moment and holds it about 0.2 s or more for a high jump (a 0.05-0.15 s tap rises 48-123 px; the step is 150 px), lets go between jumps (only a fresh press jumps), and leaves the ground inside a 0.35 s window to clear the wide gap at full speed.
setup: Desk: the robot's own table (x forward from the arm bases, y left, origin midway between them; table top 0 cm). Game controller (Xbox Wireless Controller model 1914, ABS shell, rubber stick caps, two AA cells): 15.3 x 10.2 x 6.1 cm, 287 g, lying face up with its bumpers toward the monitor in a grey PLA cradle taped to the desk (tray 11.6 x 16.7 cm, 4 mm floor, 14 mm rims with 3 mm of play round the controller, open at the back between the grips) centred at x 0.25, y 0.00; its face 4.2 cm above the desk; left stick at x 0.262, y +0.037 (cap 15.5 mm across, top 11 mm above the face, 21 degrees each way, spring-centred, 0.7 N at the cap at full throw); A button (green, 9.6 mm, 3 mm proud, 1.5 mm travel, closes at 1.0 mm with 0.4 N, opens above 0.7 mm) at x 0.251, y -0.037; B, X, Y 11 mm from the ABXY centre (x 0.262, y -0.037). Monitor (24-inch office monitor, plastic, 54.2 x 17.2 x 39.4 cm, screen 53.5 x 29.0 cm, its bottom edge 10.1 cm above the desk) standing at x 0.49 (screen face at x 0.487), y 0.00, facing the robot, showing the level of game.html (in this folder; it reads only the controller: no key moves or jumps the character, and R only restarts the level) full screen: a 1920 x 1080 picture 51.6 x 29.0 cm; ground top 200 px; the character (72 x 96 px) starts at x 130 px; a narrow gap at 520-610 px, a brick step 820-1000 px and 150 px tall, a wide gap at 1400-1700 px, a flag pole at 1830 px; three hearts (lives) at top left and four progress markers at top right. Distractors (not scored): a computer keyboard (plastic, 44.2 x 14.2 x 2.0 cm, 550 g) pushed aside at x 0.62, y +0.47, turned 17 degrees; a ceramic mug (11.4 x 9.0 x 8.0 cm, 300 g) at x 0.46, y -0.42.
scoring: The game keeps the furthest point the character reached in any of its three lives (the progress markers at the top right of the screen); a character that falls into a gap restarts at the left, and after the third fall the game shows GAME OVER and stops. 1.0: the level is cleared (the character touches the flag pole and LEVEL CLEAR shows) and afterwards, for 1 s, no gripper finger is within 3 cm of the controller, the stick is back within 3 degrees of centre and A is up (its switch open). 0.75: the character stood on the ground beyond the wide gap, or the level was cleared without that end state. 0.5: it stood on top of the brick step. 0.25: it stood on the ground beyond the narrow gap. 0: anything else. The run scores 0, whatever the game shows, if at any moment the controller moved more than 1 cm from where it lay or tilted more than 10 degrees (lifted out of its cradle), or a gripper finger came within 5 mm of the monitor's 54.2 x 17.2 x 39.4 cm outline box (stand included: from 8 cm in front of the screen's face to the back of the stand, the screen's full width, up to its top). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Restart the level in the game (the controller's Menu button, or R, in game.html; a restart sets progress back to zero, and no key can move or jump the character); the controller stays in its taped cradle and its stick and buttons spring back. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: The controller is rigid primitives at real size and mass; only its left stick (two spring-centred hinges) and face buttons (sprung sliders) move; d-pad, right stick, triggers and bumpers are fixed. The game is a Python model stepped at 20 Hz and drawn as flat shapes on the SimReady monitor's screen; game.html runs the same game in a browser with a real controller. The cradle is primitives; monitor, keyboard and mug are SimReady props.
